title: Let your yes be yes (Matthew 5:33–37)
hookLine: no oaths needed if your word is plain

cards: To be fair. Trust me. Listen to how often people add a little booster to make their words count more.
I swear I'll call you back. Honestly, I'm fine. Here's the odd thing: the more people use them, the more they suggest that without them, their words might not be true.
If I have to say honestly, what was the rest? Next in the sermon, Jesus takes on the biggest booster of his world: the oath.

teach.b: Ye have heard, he says, that you shall not break your oaths, but keep what you've sworn to the Lord. That was the law: if you swore by God, you had to keep it. But people had found loopholes.
Swear by heaven, or the earth, or Jerusalem, or your own head, and maybe it didn't count quite as much. Jesus closes every loophole. Heaven is God's throne.
The earth is his footstool. Jerusalem is the city of the great King. You can't even make one hair of your head white or black.
Everything you swear by belongs to God anyway. Then, in the King James Bible: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."
The point isn't a new rule about courtrooms.

There shouldn't be two kinds of speech: sworn words you keep, and ordinary words you don't. If your yes always means yes, you never need to swear. The letter of James repeats it: let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay.
Christians live this out in different ways.
Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians refuse to swear oaths at all, and affirm instead; that's one reason the United States Constitution lets a president swear or affirm.
Many other Christians take oaths in court or in office, reading Jesus as teaching everyday honesty, not banning every oath. Both take the heart of it seriously: a plain word, kept.
Look back at this week: peacemakers, the persecuted, salt and light, the Torah fulfilled, anger, the heart's look, and now a plain yes. Each goes deeper than the rule.

how: Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians affirm rather than swear in court, while many Christians take oaths in court or at ordination and try to keep ordinary promises as seriously as sworn ones.

games.q: people in your town swear by heaven or by Jerusalem, thinking it counts less than swearing by God. what does Jesus say?
o: swear not at all: let your yes be yes.
games.why: everything you swear by belongs to God anyway. "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay."

practice: Think back over the last day or two: where did you say yes and mean maybe, say I'm fine and mean something else, or add I swear or honestly? No guilt, just notice.
Then picture one conversation today where you say a plain yes or a plain no, and mean it, and if you pray, you can ask for a plain, true tongue.

wordCard.voice: Nai, the Greek word for yes, which Greeks still say today. Jesus closes the loopholes around oaths and asks for one kind of speech: yea, yea; nay, nay.

orig.note: Greek: yes. the yea of Matthew 5:37; Greeks still say nai for yes today.

carryVoice: Your line: yes means yes. A plain word, kept, needs no booster. A week of the sermon, done.
